transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Well, occupational health down at the precinct sent me in. They've got it in their heads that I'm not eating enough. Which, you know, the new occupational health guy they brought in, he's just a kid. Barely looks old enough to shave. He's got all these new wellness protocols for the force. Back when I joined the department in '89, nobody cared what you did as long as you could chase a guy down an alley and clear a chain-link fence. Now it's all wellness checks and stress management seminars. I told my captain, I don't need a seminar, I need the AC in my cruiser fixed. It's been making this awful rattling noise since October, and it absolutely drives me up the wall on a twelve-hour shift. 

But anyway... yeah, they're on my case because most days I just keep it to black coffee. The station coffee is basically tar, but it keeps you moving. Maybe I'll have a plain yogurt, or just a few bites of chicken at night when I get home. I don't see the big deal. If I sit down and eat a full meal, it just feels like... like I'm letting my standards slip, you know? You have to stay sharp, stay disciplined. And speaking of that, they're supposed to be issuing us these new duty belts next month that are supposed to distribute the weight better, which is fine, but the old ones were perfectly... well, anyway, that's why I'm here. Occupational health made the appointment.

You mentioned that you often stick to just black coffee or a few bites of food because you feel like eating a full meal makes you lose discipline. Has this way of eating affected your weight or energy levels recently?

Well, energy-wise, I'm fine. The coffee does the trick. But, you know, my uniform hangs off me a bit now. I've actually had to punch a couple of new holes in my belt just to keep my pants up, tighten it past the old notches. Speaking of uniforms, the quartermaster down at the precinct, Dave, he's been trying to get us all to switch to these new moisture-wicking shirts. Says they're the future of law enforcement apparel. I told him, Dave, I've been wearing the same polyester blend since the Bush administration, I'm not changing now. Plus, those new shirts snag on everything. You brush up against a brick wall and suddenly you look like you've been in a cat fight. 

Anyway, where was I? Oh, right. The nurse at occupational health, when they weighed me, she got all wide-eyed and told me my weight was dangerously low. But honestly, I looked at the number and I still thought, 'I could stand to be a little sharper.' You know, leaner. Like a greyhound. My buddy Mike, he's got a retired racing greyhound, beautiful dog. Fast as lightning, but all it does now is sleep on his couch. It's funny how things retire, isn't it?
Do you ever worry about gaining weight or find yourself actively resisting gaining any weight, even if others might tell you it's healthy to do so?

Well, yeah, I mean... worry isn't really the right word for it. It's more like a... an imperative. Like, if I step on the scale and it's up even half a pound, I get this jolt. It's like I've just completely lost control of the situation. And when you're on patrol, you can't lose control. You just can't. You have to command the scene. Like last Tuesday, we had this domestic disturbance call over on 4th and Elm. Guy was throwing lawn furniture at his neighbor's car. Just hurling patio chairs like frisbees. You show up to something like that, you can't be soft, you can't be out of shape. You have to step out of the cruiser and let them know the nonsense stops right now. 

So if I see the scale tick up, I just cut back harder that day. I absolutely cannot stand the idea of putting weight back on. It just feels sloppy. And speaking of sloppy, the paperwork they make us fill out for these domestic calls now, it's out of control. It used to be a one-page incident report, carbon copy, boom, you're done. Now it's a digital form with drop-down menus that never load right on the precinct computers. The IT guy, Kevin, he says it's a server issue, but I'm pretty sure he just spends all day playing those online video games instead of fixing the network. But yeah, no, I definitely push back hard if I think I'm gaining anything.
Do you spend a lot of time thinking about your weight or body shape, or feel that they influence how you see yourself overall?

Well, yeah, it's... it's pretty much the main thing on my mind. I mean, when I look in the mirror, I just don't see what the occupational health guy or my captain says they see. I look straight at my stomach, my waist. If I don't look lean enough, tight enough, I just... I can't respect myself that day. The whole shift is ruined. It's like my entire worth as an officer, as a man, is tied up in keeping that edge. 

Which, speaking of edges, we used to have this precinct barber, old guy named Sal. Best straight razor shave in the city. He could give you an edge up that would make you look like a million bucks for roll call. Sal retired back in '15, moved down to Boca. Now the rookies all go to these fancy salons where they serve you craft beer while you get a haircut. A haircut! I went into one once just to see, and they tried to charge me forty-five dollars for a trim. I told the kid with the sleeve tattoos, I said, 'Son, I can buy a set of clippers at the pharmacy for twenty bucks and they'll last me a decade.' 

But yeah, if I wake up and feel like there's even a fraction of an inch of slack around my waist, I just judge myself so hard. It dictates my whole mood. I have to look lean, you know? Otherwise, what's the point?

This aligns with anorexia nervosa, which is characterized by a persistent restriction of energy intake, intense fear of gaining weight, and a disturbance in self-perceived weight or shape.
